sections.overview: The African openbill is a stork found across much of sub-Saharan Africa, with an additional subspecies in north-western Madagascar. Its range follows suitable wetland habitats.
sections.identification: Adults are glossy dark birds with a long, stout bill whose mandibles meet mainly at the base and tip, leaving a conspicuous gap. Immatures are browner, duller, and have a straighter bill. Adults reach 80–94 cm and weigh about 1–1.3 kg; sources report males usually larger than females but give no sex-specific measurements.
sections.habitat: It is closely associated with fresh water, especially lake margins, marshes, river shallows, and floodplains. Trees beside wetlands provide perches and nesting sites; flooded savannas are also used when food is available.
sections.diet: Its diet consists chiefly of aquatic molluscs, including snails and freshwater bivalves. In shallow water it probes for prey, cracks snail shells with its stout bill, then cuts the attachment muscle with the pointed lower mandible.
sections.behavior: It is gregarious through the year and may gather in trees near water, yet usually searches for its slow-moving mollusc prey alone. Depending on the population, it is sedentary or makes seasonal movements.
sections.reproduction: Breeding follows the rainy season; in East Africa it is concentrated from January to March, while nesting in Zambia may occur throughout the year. Pairs build a branch-and-reed nest in a tree, lay three or four eggs, and incubate them for about 25–30 days; young leave after roughly 50–55 days.
sections.ecology: By feeding on freshwater snails and mussels, the openbill is closely tied to wetlands with abundant molluscs. Its specialized bill separates it from other storks and supports an unusually precise feeding method.
sections.conservation: The species is classified as Least Concern and is not considered globally threatened, although the English and French accounts report a continent-wide decline. Wetland loss, insecticides, hunting, and local destruction of nesting colonies are identified as pressures.
